overview:
In Jain karma theory, "sthiti-bandha" (स्थिति-बन्ध) refers to the bondage of karmic matter to the soul with respect to the *duration* (sthiti) for which that karma will remain capable of producing its results. Within the broader concept of bandha (bondage)—the mutual intermingling of jīva (soul) and karma (subtle pudgala)—sthiti-bandha is one of the four fundamental dimensions by which karmic bondage is analyzed: prakṛti-bandha (bondage by type of karma), sthiti-bandha (bondage by duration), anubhāga-bandha (bondage by intensity or fruition), and pradeśa-bandha (bondage by quantity of karmic space-points).

Sthiti in this technical sense is not merely chronological time in a conventional human sense, but a precise measure of how long a particular karmic cluster remains associated with the soul in a state capable of ripening. When karmic particles are attracted (āsrava) and transformed into specific karmas through passions (kaṣāya) and activities of mind, speech, and body, they are bound with a certain "lifespan" determined by the inner disposition (bhāva) of the soul at that moment. This determination of duration is called sthiti-bandha. The more intense and deeply rooted the passions—such as anger, pride, deceit, and greed—the longer the karmas remain bound, sometimes for extraordinarily long spans measured in Jain cosmological units.

Classical texts explain that the same external action can lead to very different sthiti-bandha depending on the internal state. A harsh act done with fleeting irritation may bind karma of relatively short duration, whereas the same act done with deliberate cruelty, sustained resentment, or strong attachment can bind karma that endures for vast stretches of time. Thus, sthiti-bandha is closely linked to the qualitative depth of one’s mental and emotional involvement in an act. It is also influenced by whether the soul possesses right faith (samyag-darśana) and restraint (saṃyama); for those on higher guṇasthānas (spiritual stages), even when karma is bound, its duration tends to be shorter due to reduced passions and greater vigilance.

From the perspective of spiritual practice, understanding sthiti-bandha clarifies why Jain ethics emphasize not only external non-violence (ahiṃsā) but also inner purification of intentions. The doctrine teaches that by cultivating equanimity (samatā), reducing attachment and aversion (rāga–dveṣa), and practicing vows and austerities, one can gradually bind karmas of shorter duration and eventually prevent new bondage (saṃvara). At advanced stages, through intense austerities and right conduct, previously bound karmas with long sthiti are brought to fruition and shed (nirjarā), while new karmas—if bound at all—have minimal duration. In this way, sthiti-bandha is a key technical concept that connects the microscopic mechanics of karmic matter with the lived discipline of Jain spiritual life.

Jain cosmological and doctrinal discussions also highlight the remarkable range of possible karmic durations. Certain karmas, such as some forms of ayuṣya (lifespan-determining karma), can have maximum sthiti spanning immense cycles of time, while others, especially for advanced aspirants, may have extremely short durations. The Tattvārtha-sūtra and its commentaries specify minimum and maximum limits for the sthiti of different karmas, showing that the system is highly structured and mathematically precise. Sthiti-bandha therefore functions as a bridge between metaphysical theory and ethical responsibility: every moment of passion or negligence not only attracts karma but also "writes" how long that karma will accompany the soul on its journey through saṃsāra.

In summary, sthiti-bandha is the aspect of karmic bondage that determines the temporal endurance of karmas attached to the soul. It depends primarily on the intensity and quality of the soul’s passions and attitudes at the time of action, and it plays a crucial role in explaining why some consequences appear quickly and pass, while others persist across many births. For the Jain practitioner, reflecting on sthiti-bandha encourages a deeper awareness of inner states, since transforming those states is the key to shortening karmic durations and ultimately ending bondage altogether.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation:
“Bondage (bandha) is (of four kinds): according to the nature (prakṛti), duration (sthiti), intensity of fruition (anubhāga), and quantity of space-points (pradeśa) of karma.
Wrong belief, non-abstinence, negligence, and passions are the causes of bondage.”
primary_sources.notes: These sūtras (commonly cited as Tattvārtha-sūtra 8.3 and 8.1) provide the canonical classification of karmic bondage and its causes. Sthiti-bandha is explicitly named as one of the four dimensions of bandha. Later commentaries—both Digambara and Śvetāmbara—elaborate how the inner states of the soul at the time of action determine the duration (sthiti) for which karmas remain bound, and they specify minimum and maximum limits for different karmas.

primary_sources.title: Samayasāra
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda
primary_sources.translation: “One who is endowed with right faith is free from karmic bondage.”
primary_sources.notes: Although this verse speaks generally of freedom from karma-bandha, traditional expositions use it to contrast the mundane soul, which binds karma with specific prakṛti, sthiti, anubhāga, and pradeśa, with the right-believing soul progressing toward states where new bondage—especially of long duration—is increasingly curtailed. In commentarial literature, the reduction of sthiti-bandha is treated as a key effect of right faith and diminishing passions.

primary_sources.title: Bhagavatī-sūtra (Vyākhyāprajñapti)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Mahāvīra’s teachings preserved by gaṇadharas
primary_sources.translation: “With all (their units), all souls bind karma.”
primary_sources.notes: This passage, cited in traditional discussions of bandha, emphasizes that the soul binds karma through all its units at once. In later doctrinal analysis, this comprehensive binding is further described in terms of the fourfold structure of bandha, including sthiti-bandha. The idea that every unit of the soul can be associated with karmic particles underlines the vast potential range of karmic durations, which are then technically specified as sthiti.

misconceptions.myth: Sthiti-bandha is just the ordinary passage of time and has nothing to do with one’s inner state.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain doctrine, sthiti-bandha is a precise karmic determination of how long specific karmas remain bound to the soul, and it is directly shaped by the intensity and quality of the soul’s passions, attitudes, and level of spiritual development at the moment of action. Two similar external actions can result in very different karmic durations depending on the inner disposition.

misconceptions.myth: Once the duration (sthiti) of a karma is fixed, spiritual practice cannot affect it until it naturally expires.
misconceptions.reality: While classical texts do set minimum and maximum limits for karmic durations, they also teach that through austerities, repentance, and right conduct, karmas can be brought to early fruition and shed (nirjarā). Moreover, by transforming one’s inner states, future karmas—if bound at all—will have shorter sthiti. Thus, spiritual practice is central both to reducing new sthiti-bandha and to managing existing karmas.

misconceptions.myth: Sthiti-bandha is a minor technical detail relevant only to scholars, not to lay or ascetic practice.
misconceptions.reality: Sthiti-bandha is deeply connected to everyday ethical and spiritual life. It explains why sustained anger, greed, or deceit can bind long-lasting karmas, while moments of equanimity and restraint bind little or no new karma. Understanding this encourages practitioners to pay attention to their inner states, not just outward behavior, as a way to shorten karmic durations and progress toward liberation.
